newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cambodian minister says Khmer Rouge days are over.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian minister says Khmer Rouge days are over.

text.p: Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot on Friday gave an upbeat assessment of stability in his country, and said the threat posed by the Khmer Rouge was all but over.
Huot, on a visit to inaugurate a new embassy building in Tokyo, said Cambodia's economic and political development was proceeding apace.
He made no mention of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's rejection on Friday of an offer to join an alliance headed by his main rival in the coalition government.

Speaking at the opening of his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) congress, Hun Sen said the CPP wanted to continue working with the royalist FUNCINPEC party of First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh in government and parliament.
But he ruled out an alliance with FUCINPEC and denied there were plans by the CPP to form its own alliance, saying the CPP "is a big party and we cannot accept to join with any front".
Nevertheless, Hun Sen confirmed that representatives from former Khmer Rouge military units were attending the CPP's four-day congress.
Huot told a news conference that time had run out for the Khmer Rouge, which had been hit hard by defections to the government side.
"The Khmer Rouge are going to be gone before the end of this year," Huot told a news conference.
The hardline Maoist group presided over Cambodia from 1975 to 1979 in a reign of terror that left more than one million people dead.
Huot said no one knew whether Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot was alive or dead and it no longer mattered because he was a spent force.
"All I'll say is that Pol Pot is a sick man in mind and body," Huot said.
He said Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk, whose presence was regarded as a key stabilising force in Cambodia, was in "good health for a man 74 years old".
But Huot said the King could no longer travel around the countryside as much as before because of his treatment for cancer.
Huot refused to give an exact date for local elections due this year and for general elections due in 1998, but indicated the local polls might be held over a month instead of on one day.
"Local elections may not be held on a single day but might instead be held province-by-province over a month," he said.
Huot said Cambodia would again need United Nations and other international help in monitoring both elections to ensure they were fair.
He urged Japan and other nations to invest in Cambodia, saying everything except heavy industry was needed.
"My message is that Cambodia is open for business to everyone," Huot said.
